26px;font-size: 16px;">Today I’m going to do something a little different. I’m going to tell you what I think the debate over GDP is really about.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Free trade usually raises GDP. Immigration, done right, raises GDP.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> Rightists in America want less free trade and less immigration. But every time they propose restricting trade and immigration, someone — either libertarian business/econ types on their own side, or moderate liberals on the other side — says “That will make America poorer!”. So they want some way to neutralize this objection, so they can do things that will, in fact, make America poorer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So America’s right borrowed an argument from the European left. The European left </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dc646ee1-3c84-45f1-b112-c192f3e136b4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">favors degrowth</a><span>, and another term for degrowth is “making GDP go down on purpose”. So naturally, they’re always trying to find reasons to denigrate GDP as a metric of human flourishing (see </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/370ac5f9-ed6c-4434-9725-ab9901014d6f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7056c82b-0597-4de8-bd16-dc15336046e7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b179091-2573-43e8-adaa-ea316131348a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span> for examples). The American right is simply tweaking these arguments to make them more appealing to their own base. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>JD Vance, who has emerged as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce674a3f-c641-4901-a070-07221bc9e73d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the consensus leader of the New Right</a><span>, makes </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/84c68cd3-6e35-4f53-9e1b-7fc77d10b443?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a bunch of these anti-GDP arguments</a><span> in his new book. For example, he uses the example of Japan to point out that unobserved quality differences in non-traded products can make it difficult to compare GDP across countries:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re focused on GDP, a $6 pint of Japanese strawberries is no different from a $6 pint of American strawberries. If you’re focused on dollars and cents, each contributes equally to the economic indicators. But if everyone in Japan eats better strawberries than everyone in America, the economic indicators have failed to measure something meaningful.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is actually a good argument, and I’ve made it myself many times in the past. I’m in Japan right now, and there actually are a lot of little things that make Japanese products and services a bit nicer than their American counterparts — clean tables at Starbucks, slightly better-tasting food, and so on. Economists who try to adjust for quality differences end up catching some of these things, but probably miss most of them. That ends up </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dcc5988e-9630-4184-a5ea-0fc117e84fa8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">creating a problem</a><span> for GDP comparisons between countries. And it’s only one of many such problems. Comparing lifestyles in countries where life is very different is just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/83a6a2a8-71e8-418c-8ca1-bf690aeb1b35?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a difficult thing to do</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But instead of simply noting that economics is hard, JD Vance uses this good argument as a reason to bash the entire field of economics:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When I got back home, a friend asked me if I learned anything on my trip to Japan. “Yes,” I replied snidely. “Maybe economics is just fake.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When you read some of Vance’s other arguments against GDP, his agenda becomes clearer:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[A]s the decline of Christianity has left us without a shared moral language, economics has stepped into the vacuum. We pretend there are scientific answers to questions of values. Take one of the major issues of the 2024 campaign and a significant focus of our time in the White House: Should our trade policy be oriented around protecting domestic industries and jobs or around ensuring a short-term supply of cheap consumer goods?</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This idea — that economists urge values of base consumerism on society, and ignore other moral considerations — is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7d9af42a-9ffd-4495-8348-56a1b5964ad0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">common in European leftist discourse</a><span>. But instead of urging us to care more about inequality, power, and so on, as European leftists do, Vance wants us to care more about spiritual elevation, morality, community — i.e., things that the American right cares about. He goes on to write:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[W]e now live in a society almost blinded to considerations outside of the economic. This way of thinking is inherently opposed to the Christian way, which demands more focus on people…Take, for instance, the time we spend with our children…Domestic labor—that done by moms and dads—if unpaid, is uncounted in measures like GDP. When I leave work to spend time with my children, when I cook them dinner or argue with them about eating their carrots, I am engaged in economically unproductive work. No money changes hands, so it doesn’t show up in our national figures. By contrast, if I left for dinner at 6 p.m. and returned to work until midnight while paying a total stranger to look after my kid, my contribution to GDP would be much higher.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">and:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you step away from the glory of economic statistics, so much of American life has gone wrong. An influx of prescription opioids became a flood of synthetic opioids, which has led to tens of thousands of deaths each year and a declining life expectancy among a substantial portion of our society. We have made great progress on reducing infant mortality, but we send our children into a world—even in the physical security of their own homes—that bombards them with images and influences that have left them isolated, depressed, and increasingly at risk of self-harm. We are more disconnected, lonely, and isolated, even in the midst of historic levels of material comfort.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">All this economic abundance coexists with intense spiritual misery. We orient people toward a life of consumption. We tell them to find meaning in the home they buy, the money they earn, the prestige of their job. We bombard them with all manner of creature comforts, and add their consumption—price club mega-size junk—to our national GDP. We use that GDP as a yardstick for our broader society, which is why it’s possible for false prophet economists to argue the American Dream is healthy even as suicide and addiction rates soar and the laughter of children fades from our streets.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some of these arguments are — in my opinion — reasonable. A culture of overwork can boost GDP, at least in the short term, at the expense of quality time with family. This is actually a common argument of the center-left, which is why liberals have long fought — often successfully — for </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/356c5d6e-c69d-41dd-941e-6bd753f9ed2a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">more paid family leave</a><span> and other policies that reduce GDP slightly in exchange for more quality time with family. Whether this has increased birth rates isn’t clear — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/14d943db-2654-45c8-b789-8f11237869db?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the evidence is very mixed</a><span> — but it’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cb254f97-ecc8-496a-bc75-6f3b8e1375cf?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a very popular policy</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other arguments are clearly mistaken. Over-prescription of opioids has clearly </span><em>reduced</em><span> GDP, by a massive amount. Yes, selling a bunch of opioid painkillers to Americans </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/139e81a6-5117-4d7d-89a5-80bbeb6163e7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">raises GDP by a few billion dollars</a><span>, but this is vastly outweighed by the trillions of dollars of GDP that we lose from having a bunch more people addicted to painkillers, heroin, and fentanyl. Here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3aa0c662-d6f4-4d12-8f40-025225f7d4fa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the Philadelphia Fed in 2023</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is growing evidence that the opioid epidemic has harmed many aspects of the real economy, including the labor market, consumer finance, and municipal finance. According to analyses from the Council of Economic Advisers’ 2019 report, the annual (nominal) </span><strong>economic cost of the opioid epidemic</strong><span>, including the cost of lives lost, is estimated at about $700 billion (roughly 3.4 percent of GDP) in 2018 alone, and </span><strong>over $2.5 trillion from 2015 to 2018</strong><span>. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So if you care about GDP, you should view curbing opioid and opiate abuse as a huge priority! Vance is simply not thinking about this very clearly. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Vance’s real problem is that he conflates correlation with causation. In words that could have come straight from the mouth of a European degrowther, he rails against “creature comforts”, “consumption”, and “price club mega-size junk”. But nowhere does he explain why </span><em>depriving</em><span> Americans of these creature comforts would give them closer-knit families, a stronger sense of morality, stronger communities, reduced loneliness, and so on. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why would taking away Americans’ large houses, SUVs, big-screen TVs, or central air conditioning make them spiritually richer? Modern Europe — which JD Vance </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e46f74e3-98e6-4cce-99ed-e9eaaf8f2ab7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">spends much of his time railing against</a><span> — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/83a6a2a8-71e8-418c-8ca1-bf690aeb1b35?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">lacks most of these things</a><span>. And yet America has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/70005918-de11-496a-b1b5-32db8c2fbd65?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">higher fertility rates than Europe</a><span>, we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9c121b87-91e6-420c-bd65-d86b2423c596?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">go to church much more</a><span>, and we have a much more robust social conservative movement. Europe has also been far more restrictive of speech that criticizes Islam, as Vance repeatedly notes. Yes, America has been trending </span><em>away</em><span> from social conservatism and Christianity in recent decades, but so has Europe, and the gap remains. Other developed countries in East Asia — most of which are moderately poorer than the U.S. in GDP terms — are extremely secular. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What about America’s past? We were much poorer in the 1950s, yet we went to church a lot more, had larger families, and so on. If you took away the material gains we’ve made since then, would we go back to tradwives and bowling leagues and lawn parties and Sunday church and 4 kids per family? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Perhaps, but it’s doubtful. Remember that the 1950s and 1960s were the culmination of a long </span><em>upswing</em><span> of community, religiosity, and so on in American society — something the sociologist Robert Putnam </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/08cbf009-4a98-4d53-9237-3c95c591ee63?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">has documented extensively</a><span>. Church attendance rose:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table comforts” that Vance despises — the single-family homes, the cars, the televisions, the lawns, and so on. The image of that material prosperity, depicted in glossy ads and paintings from the time, is a powerful part of 1950s nostalgia. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, many economists argue that one big cause of the Baby Boom was the fact that economic growth — bigger houses, better medical care, new labor-saving devices like washing machines, refrigerators, and vacuums, and so on — made it easier and cheaper to raise kids. This is from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a7941e6-3a21-4022-8330-c3c317598559?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a relevant </a><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a7941e6-3a21-4022-8330-c3c317598559?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Works in Progress</a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a7941e6-3a21-4022-8330-c3c317598559?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> article</a><span> by Anvar Sarygulov & Phoebe Arslanagic-Little:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Parenthood rapidly became much easier and safer between the 1930s and 1950s. The spread of labour-saving devices in the home such as washing machines and fridges made raising children easier; improvements in medicine making childbirth safer; and easier access to housing made it cheaper to house larger families…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[H]ousehold electrification paved the way for other technologies, including home refrigeration…By the 1940s, electric washing machines were becoming normal in middle class homes…</span><span>Between 1936 and 1956, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ad7a3feb-719e-4070-b4e6-2f3da1f7d35a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">America’s</a><span> maternal death rate fell by 94 percent, from 51 deaths per 10,000 live births to under 3…[M]edical advances, which were being made across the West, radically reduced the most serious potential cost faced by prospective mothers: life itself…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Alongside strides forward in household and medical technology…[I]t became easier to secure a home in which to raise children. The number of houses built soared across the West after World War Two…This house-building bonanza led to sharp rises in homeownership rates.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The golden thread linking the phenomena that comprise the triple mechanism we describe above – advances in household technology, progress in medical technology, and easier access to housing – is that they together </span><strong><span>sharply reduced the cost of having children</span></strong><span>. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you like the kind of society we had in 1960, you can’t ignore the story of how we got to 1960. The answer was “economic growth”. This, combined with the examples of Europe and Asia, is why there’s no reason to believe that forcing Americans to be poorer — taking away the “creature comforts” Vance despises — would lead us to suddenly rediscover the value of community, family, and religion. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now it’s worth noting that if you were to decrease America’s GDP to poor-country levels — below $15,000 per person, as opposed to over $90,000 today — you might be able to raise fertility. That’s how low you have to go before most countries have fertility above replacement level:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px Also, I kind of doubt that JD Vance wants to force Americans to live lives similar to those lived in Sub-Saharan Africa.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What about JD Vance’s preferred policies — trade protectionism and immigration reduction? Would those restore American community, family, and religion, at the expense of a bit of GDP? As I said earlier, that’s actually what I think this whole debate is really about. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On trade, you’ve seen Trump explicitly make the argument that Americans are going to need to suffer a bit of material deprivation in order to achieve the administration’s goals:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/7c677185-79b2-4e08-af5c-5ae13a2fe081?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/2eJv810QWOs" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But how will doing this restore community, family, etc.? But as Bryan Caplan and many others </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3497096f-a674-4361-8d42-e42ab0dbae02?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">have pointed out</a><span>, the effect size is tiny — in Putnam’s research, going from </span><em>zero</em><span> diversity to </span><em>maximum</em><span> diversity reduces social trust by the equivalent of 1 point on a 100-point scale. This suggests that all the mass deportations in the world won’t move the needle on American community and togetherness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, JD Vance’s crusade against GDP is a </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d99a74ee-670d-48e8-be51-740836409af6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">cargo cult</a></em><span>. Sure, GDP doesn’t measure “the beauty of our poetry or the strength of our marriages,” to use Robert F. Kennedy’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/69177737-0744-45c4-9c5d-d2a3fe62e4bb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">famous words</a><span>. But that doesn’t mean that making Americans poorer will make their poetry more beautiful or their marriages stronger. Nor does it mean that policies that also happen to make us a bit poorer, like immigration reduction or tariffs, are any more likely to strengthen our society. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a famous episode of </span><em>Star Trek: The Next Generation</em><span> — my favorite TV show of all time — Captain Picard castigates an alien for turning his society into a fascist empire. When the alien responds that the fascist government’s forced modernization program raised his daughter out of poverty, Picard responds with the beautiful quote at the top of this post: “Her belly may be full, but her spirit will be empty.” But was Picard arguing that it was</span><em> the full bellies themselves</em><span> that emptied the people’s spirits? Was he merely arguing that the fascist empire ought to become a </span><em>poorer</em><span> fascist empire, in order to restore the virtue of the people? Only a fool would think so. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Look, I also want America to have a stronger society. I want us to have more kids. I want us to have more stable families. I want us to have closer-knit communities, better moral values, etc. But that doesn’t mean the New Right knows how to get us there. So far, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b0dc466-d194-45ae-9ffe-7132c9210b48?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the New Right has built nothing</a><span> — no new community organizations or institutions, no religious revival, nothing that would knit our society together. It has merely thrashed and thrashed against modernity, with no plan for a replacement. JD Vance’s crusade against GDP is simply more of the same.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: 10px;">“Done right” means getting immigrants who, on average, earn more than the native-born. This raises GDP by a composition effect — you have richer people on average. It also probably raises GDP by other means — increasing market size which increases returns to scale, boosting innovation and entrepreneurship, and so on. If you get mostly low-skilled immigrants, things get dicier — the composition effect reduces GDP because you’re importing poorer people, but the increased market size may still cancel that out. But in general, if you want higher per capita GDP, you should be selective in terms of who you let into the country. Total GDP, of course, is a different matter — if you want a bigger country, in order to be more powerful in military terms, then letting in tons of low-skilled immigrants may be worth it even if they reduce per capita GDP. And of course, there are distributional reasons to allow in low-skilled immigration — eldercare and so on. But basically, if you let in high-skilled immigrants, your society gets richer by pretty much every metric.</p></div></div></div></div><table class="email-ufi-2-bottom" role="presentation" the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/98c24055-8d20-4d30-9a9e-63f844b97b24?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Wall Street Journal</a><span> describes a tense meeting among European leaders early this year, convened after Donald Trump threatened to use military force to seize Greenland from Denmark. According to the </span><em><span>Journal</span></em><span>,</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>heads of government were venting so emotionally about the 47th president that some of the nearly 30 leaders present would later call the session “therapy night.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yesterday, soon after he arrived in Ankara for the NATO Summit, Trump reiterated his demand that Denmark hand him </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d191d648-5f8d-48e9-ad20-5e645d256221?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">control of Greenland</a><span>.</span><span> But reactions were subdued. As far as I can tell, our erstwhile allies are now treating Trump as the senile uncle who says crazy, outrageous things, but shouldn’t be taken seriously.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What has changed? According to the </span><em><span>Journal</span></em><span>, European leaders have largely given up on hopes that they can bring back the America they used to know, and are quietly, in effect, declaring independence:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>American allies have begun pushing the gas pedal on an unprecedented experiment in de-Americanization. Authorities from France to the Netherlands are quietly removing American tech from their systems, adopting European open-source software and urging civil servants to no longer use Microsoft Teams or Office. Belatedly, they are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to try to boost Europe’s own private space firms, AI companies, and data centers, to avoid leaning on U.S. juggernauts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Europeans are running studies on where they would store their data or process their payments should friction with the U.S. escalate, and how well their American-made weaponry would operate without Washington’s authorization. Nations whose empires once spanned the globe are now stuck trying to extricate themselves from their humbling dependency on American technology and military power, without provoking the U.S.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Their willingness to de-Americanize partly reflects recognition that reconciliation is hopeless: Trump is who he is, and a nation that elected him twice simply can’t be trusted.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, Europe’s turn away from Trump also reflects plummeting perceptions of his power. At one time t</span><span>he world </span><span>feared Trump although it </span><span>never respected </span><span>him. The silence that met his renewed demand for Greenland shows that the world no longer takes him seriously.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>America </span><span>remains </span><span>an economic superpower with an enormous military budget. And the combination of a supine Republican Party</span><span>, along with</span><span> a </span><span>Supreme Court that </span><span>shamelessly </span><span>greenlights Trump’s authoritarianism, has given this president more control over</span><span> U.S. policy than any president has ever had, or ever should have. But </span><span>while Trump is able to run roughshod over Americans, he can no longer bully the rest of the world. Thanks to Trump, </span><span>the U.S. </span><span>has seen its global influence plunge.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are three big reasons for that precipitous decline.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, there is the debacle in Iran. Not only did Trump’s war of choice fail in all its objectives, it revealed that U.S. military power is far more limited than almost anyone realized. The insistence by Trump and his lackeys that this humiliating defeat was a great victory </span><span>shows that American foreign policy only serves to pander to Trump’s fragile ego. And when his ego meets reality, it slithers away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In addition to showing the limits of U.S. military power, the war also showed the limits of U.S. financial power: It is increasingly easy for nations to bypass U.S. banks and the dollar using cryptocurrency — and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/550255d6-0a41-4aed-97a3-fb4cca92bb41?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Chinese yuan</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A second, in its way equally important, blow to U.S. prestige and influence has been Trump’s failure to deliver Ukraine to Vladimir Putin.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For make no mistake: everyone at that summit in Ankara knows that Trump, JD Vance and company both expected and hoped that their betrayal of Ukraine would lead to Russian victory. Surely, they imagined, Ukraine would be unable to hold off the onslaught from its much bigger neighbor without U.S. aid</span><span>. To America’s everlasting shame, </span><span>Trump told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that he didn’t “have the cards.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yet after Trump </span><span>cut U.S. aid to Ukraine by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b46fd008-e8a7-4a67-81a7-f9fef75d5658?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">99 percent</a><span>, Ukraine not only survived</span><span> but</span><span> began gaining the upper hand. Europe has stepped up financially, more or less replacing the lost American dollars. And Ukrainian military innovation has largely made up for the loss of American weapons.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The result has been to make </span><span>the U.S. increasingly</span><span> irrelevant. Put it this way: Iran taught foreign governments not to fear American might; </span><span>China, along with the crypto industry, has taught rogue countries that they needn’t fear American financial control; and</span><span> Ukraine has taught foreign governments that they don’t need American support</span><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Finally, Trump’s global power play rested on economics even more than on military force, above all on his belief that other nations would cower in fear at the prospect of facing U.S. tariffs. But Trump’s attempt to weaponize international trade has been a bust. Most notably, China’s economy has powered right through the Trump tariffs. Furthermore, it turns out that China has escalation dominance in the trade war: we need their rare earths more than they need access to our consumers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And other nations — even Canada and Mexico, which have historically been highly dependent on the U.S. market — are moving to reduce their dependence. Canada’s move to build a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fef0073e-355f-4107-83d0-ff937f507772?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">new pipeline</a><span> that will let it sell Alberta oil to Asia rather than the Midwest is just a highly visible symbol of a general world move toward bypassing America now that we have become an unstable, unreliable economic partner.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The combined effect of these humiliations for Trump and his minions has been a drastic reordering of America’s place in the world. For most of last year foreign leaders kept trying, desperately, to appease Trump. These days they’re mostly just humoring him, building a world in which his sundowning won’t matter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s extremely unlikely that anything substantive will come out of this NATO meeting. And a year ago the prospect of a failed summit would have been a source of deep concern. Now it will be met with a shrug: Nobody expects anything but chaotic bluster from Trump, and what he does matters less and less.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><em><span>Note: I’ll be doing a Substack Live at noon with Heather Cox Richardson</span></em></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. The Biden administration alienated a lot of voters by governing far to the left on domestic issues and, while Kamala Harris did turn things around from her dire starting position, it was unwise of Democrats to pick a candidate so closely associated with Joe Biden and doubly unwise of that candidate to do so little to distance herself from Biden on any domestic issues. A repeated pattern in American politics is that when a party loses by being too extreme, their initial reaction is to become even more extreme. Democrats </span><em><span>ought</span></em><span> to move to the center in 2028, but they probably won’t and that’s bad.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But that’s not Marshall’s argument.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead, he’s arguing that the center is getting what it deserves for being insufficiently committed to the fight against Donald Trump and MAGA. And I think that this is wrong. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Rather, it’s the hard left that is taking advantage of the Democratic Party’s current weakened state to advance all-out factional warfare as their top priority, above fighting Trump. style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And note that the people they’re challenging are </span><em><span>not</span></em><span> particularly Which is just to say, by all means, you should endorse the expenditure of time and attention and resources needed to fight safe-seat primary battles against incumbents who are way too left-wing to win races in Iowa and Texas and Ohio </span><em><span>if you actually agree with the candidates challenging them</span></em><span>. But if your focus is on beating Trump, then admit to yourself that you hold an uncool and somewhat unfashionable set of political priorities and simply disagree with the hottest youth movement in America. Don’t run cover for people who have a different worldview from yours and hope for the best.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Do you want to fight or do you want to win?</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the TV show “Andor” — the best recent art about politics — Diego Luna as the lead character observes, “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88c5bee0-4d18-4aba-ac3e-8663ec76712f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>We’re in a war. You wanna fight, or do you wanna win?</span></a><span>”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And I think that this is a question I am constantly asking my “Politix” Co-Host Brian Beutler to look into his heart and ponder. Because for the last few years, it really seems to me that for many Democrats, the answer is that they want to fight. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Or, rather, that politics is primarily expressive behavior and their priority in politics is </span><em><span>expressing</span></em><span> their strong dislike of Donald Trump. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s understandable. The United States of America is a nation of individualists. We are also a wealthy society in which most people are living very far from subsistence levels. Most American college graduates, in particular, enjoy a level of material comfort that is inconceivable to most people around the world or throughout human history. Most of us choose jobs and careers that give us not just money but also a sense of self-actualization and value. Politics is becoming more post-material in almost every affluent country. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The United States is unusual, though, in maintaining a strong two-party system. You’re seeing fragmentation in lots of foreign countries, where voters increasingly prioritize the idea of voting for a political party that they feel really speaks for them rather than one that tries to speak for the median voter even if the ultimate outcome is just going to be a coalition deal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I don’t want to claim to be above expressive politics. I really love Green Day, and I think there’s something exhilarating about being in a crowd of people chanting, “no Trump, no K.K.K., no fascist U.S.A.”</span></p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c8387397-f412-49f4-8ed6-32303f3d716b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/varExpTrTb8" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Wouldn’t it feel awesome if I could watch a politician who I feel as good about as I feel about Green Day? A speech that gave me the vibes of a great concert. That </span><em><span>would</span></em><span> be awesome. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I have to temper myself and remember that Mary Peltola, James Talarico, Josh Turek, Sherrod Brown, and Roy Cooper have a weighty responsibility on their shoulders. What’s more, Green Day borrowed the slogan from a more obscure punk band called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/206865ac-bd27-4e38-ae49-42cc6b4ee4cd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>MDC</span></a><span>, an acronym whose meaning has changed over the years but has often stood for Millions of Dead Cops, which is not a great electoral message.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s fun for Graham Platner to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ca843301-0c2f-4e81-a207-8c358d9f3a5f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>campaign with the Dropkick Murphys</span></a><span>, but that’s just another way of saying that expressive politics in blue states is more fun than winning over swing voters. Meanwhile, it turns out that the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/526b5c58-3ab7-414e-afd2-c76c83e7ed09?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>unfun people wringing their hands</span></a><span> about his bad judgement were on to something important. I get why the deeply idiosyncratic people who believe that the benefits of living in New York City exceed the financial costs find it more joyful to participate in Zohran Mamdani’s campaign against Andrew Cuomo than to care about Cait Conley beating an incumbent Republican in the suburbs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it drives me crazy when I see professional political operatives, staffers, and media personalities who happen to be college-educated urbanites treating things like “excitement” and “attention” as if they are wholly exogenous rather than things influential people construct. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If you work in these fields and are </span><em><span>choosing</span></em><span> to be more excited about and pay more attention to politicians who appeal to your social peers than to politicians who appeal to the older, less-credentialed, and dramatically less-urbanized population of swing voters, then that is a decision </span><em><span>you</span></em><span> are making about what’s important in American life today. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think that defeating the MAGA movement is important. I also think that providing health insurance to low-income people by winning power in red states and expanding Medicaid is important. So even though Cooper and Andy Beshear and John Bel Edwards in some sense do not speak directly to my personal tastes, I choose in my capacity as a professional political pundit to treat their work as important and interesting and exciting. Because it </span><em><span>is</span></em><span> important, and because if you can’t find it within yourself to be excited by and interested in the people doing important work, then I don’t understand why you’re in these fields at all.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Know when to walk away and know when to run</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Progressive candidates waging factional battles in safe-seat primaries have defined themselves as the true heroes of the Resistance by the sleight of hand of engaging in maximalist anti-Trump position-taking. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, Trump has done bad, cruel things on immigration policy. Democrats should (and largely do) oppose that. But leftists argue that the way to </span><em><span>maximally</span></em><span> oppose Trump on immigration is to refuse to own up to any problems with Biden-era admissions, say that we should “abolish ICE,” or perhaps agree with Avila Chevalier that “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d959912-9384-4629-8caa-4468c6b63480?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>all deportations are wrong</span></a><span>.” </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Brad Lander recently won a primary against an incumbent House Democrat in Manhattan. By my lights, whatever the substantive differences between Lander and Dan Goldman, the whole idea of spending time and money and resources on something like that is very different from spending time and money and resources on fighting Trump. But Lander’s argument was that the primary was in fact part of a larger battle between “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bfa21da5-89fb-4abe-887e-2c1b5989d639?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>fighters and folders</span></a><span>.” That’s a clever way of getting normal resistance-oriented Democrats to ignore the fact that Lander’s whole campaign was a diversion of resources away from anti-Trump politics and into ideological rigorism. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Because, by definition, if you are dogmatically left-wing, you will be opposed to anything Trump proposes even if it’s extremely popular or makes sense on the merits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I used to play regularly in a friendly poker game, and I was never very good at it. The reason is that I’d get bored and play way too many hands. I was </span><em><span>aware</span></em><span> that this was bad strategy and would sporadically resolve to do better, but after a beer or two I’d be feeling loose and happy. My discipline would collapse and I’d be playing expressive poker rather than smart poker.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Which is just to say that if you’re trying to win then, as the song says, “You got to know when to hold ’em and know when to fold ’em.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From my perspective as someone who wants to win, the big problem with establishment Democrats is that they’re not folding enough hands. When you insist on fighting Trump on questions like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ba3e93ab-d212-40ab-a231-216c59a86a84?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>who should play on women’s sports teams</span></a><span> or whether you </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0f9754e7-a867-446e-ab65-6c617305e53e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>should need an ID to vote</span></a><span>, you are not playing to win. It’s the establishment that owns that mistake, not the left, but the left </span><em><span>does</span></em><span> keep them pinned down by demanding even more losing fights on questions like ICE. From the left’s viewpoint, this is at least rational because they are sincerely not focused on beating Republicans — that’s why they’re pouring so much energy into beating Democratic incumbents in primaries. And they are enabled in this internecine extravagance and waste by resistance-minded people like Marshall who prioritize “fighting” over playing to win.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><strong>Transcript</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yesterday, Donald Trump ordered Scott Bessent, the Secretary of theTreasury, to cut off all trade with Spain. Bessent said “Yes, sir.” Trump also said that this is because the Spaniards had stolen his strawberries. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Okay, I made up that second part, but he did in fact order Bessent to cut off all trade. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is not going to happen.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Presidents have a lot of discretionary authority on tariffs and trade, more than they should, but you do not have the right as president to impose tariffs on a country just because you don’t like their defense spending or you think that they haven’t been nice enough to you.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So this would not fly even in the Trump administration. Even with a supine congress and a permissive Supreme Court this is not going to happen. Also Spain is part of the European Union. So this is like Europe declaring “we’re cutting off all trade with Florida”: they can’t do that. And also, there’s a lot of U.S. business with Spain. In fact, Spain is one of those countries with which we run a trade surplus. So U.S. business would be howling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So this is all a non-event, this is is not something that is real. Except that the President of the United States did say this. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was completely crazy, and that’s the story that we should be taking from this. It’s not really at this point about economics. It doesn’t even make sense to talk about Trump Administration policies, let alone ideology. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What we have is President Sundowner. I mean, this this is completely insane stuff. In any kind of normally functioning political system, in any kind of normally functioning party environment we would have a massive bipartisan call across the aisle, across almost everybody except for a handful of members of congress who are themselves crazy, to say okay this guy is non compos mentis. We cannot leave the fate of the United States or the world in the hands of somebody who is completely irrational, who is making demands and believing himself to have powers that he does not. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And of course, instead, not only does everybody pretend that he’s still a rational human being, but the Republican Party, the Trump administration, is full-on engaged in trying to build a personality cult.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What this says to me is that the problem is a lot bigger than Trump. Something is fundamentally wrong with America, and at this point you don’t have to go through complicated justifications. You can just say something is wrong with a country and a system that lets this guy remain in a position of power.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Have a good day.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman.
